Package org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.lang

Class Parser

java.lang.Object
org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.lang.Parser
public final class Parser extends Object
The Mandela parser: a recursive-descent parser that turns source text into a list of statements.

Two entry points, because two very different hosts consume it:

  • parseStrict(java.lang.String, java.lang.String) for the command line and the embedding API — throws LangException at the first problem.
  • parse(java.lang.String, java.lang.String) for editors — never throws. It reports every error it can, resynchronising at the next statement boundary after each one, so a single typo does not hide the rest of the file. That is what lets Espresso paint a full Problems list while the author is mid-edit.

The parser also enforces the contextual rules the grammar cannot express: break/continue only inside a loop, return only inside a function, this/super only inside a class. Those are reported here rather than at compile time because the position of the mistake is exactly what an editor needs to show.

Instances are not thread-safe and are used once.

    • expectStatementEnd

      protected void expectStatementEnd()
      Requires a separator after a statement: a newline, ;, the end of a block, or end of file. Anything else is a missing separator, which is the single most common Mandela syntax error and so gets its own message.

    • block

      protected Ast.Stmt.Block block()
      Parses { stmt* } into a Ast.Stmt.Block. Newlines directly after the opening brace, and before each statement, are skipped.

    • condition

      protected Ast.Expr condition(String construct)
      Parses the condition of if / while / match.

      Both spellings are accepted: the parenthesised one Java and C authors reach for, and the Kotlin-style bare expression. A condition is always followed by a &#123; or a value, never by another statement, so dropping the parentheses cannot make the grammar ambiguous.

      A condition that is missing altogether gets its own message. Left to the expression parser, if &#123; 1 &#125; reads its body as a map literal and complains about a map key, which sends the author looking at the wrong half of the line.

      Parameters:
      construct - the keyword being parsed, for the error text
      Returns:
      the condition expression
